summary: Teach diffusion (ages 12–13) as the NET movement of particles from higher to lower concentration, arising from random motion in both directions, continuing to a dynamic equilibrium with no energy input. Ground the invisible mechanism in an observed macroscopic spreading (including a still cold vs still hot beaker comparison), build a directional particle model, derive the three rate factors (steeper gradient, larger surface area, shorter diffusion distance) by controlled variation, and apply it to real cell contexts (O₂/CO₂ at alveoli, glucose into respiring cells). A live particle simulation is the preferred vehicle because net flow emerging from random motion is a dynamic process; static diagrams, a 3D alveolar scene, and a checking quiz are retained as distinct supports with stated limits.
misconceptions: Thinking diffusion stops once concentrations are equal because particles stop moving — in fact motion continues; only NET movement is zero (dynamic equilibrium).
Believing particles are actively 'pushed' or 'want' to spread out, rather than moving randomly with a statistical net drift down the gradient.
Confusing diffusion (of any particle down its own gradient) with osmosis (net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane).
Thinking diffusion needs energy from the cell (it is passive) — confusing it with active transport.
Assuming diffusion only happens in gases, not in liquids/solutions.

activities.title: Observed spreading then the particle picture
steps: Drop a spot of food colouring (or a tea bag) into a beaker of still COLD water and, separately, into a beaker of still HOT water; watch both for several minutes without stirring and compare how far the colour spreads. Diffusion alone takes a long time to spread colour evenly through a whole beaker (possibly hours or longer), so check back later instead of waiting for it to finish in one lesson.
State predictions first: will the dye spread at all without stirring, in which beaker will it spread faster, and why?
Draw a before/after particle picture: particles crowded on one side at the start, evenly spread at the end.
Describe in words why the colour spreads on its own, using the idea of particles moving by themselves.
activities.insight: Diffusion happens on its own with no stirring or energy input because particles are already in constant random motion; the net spreading is driven by there being more particles in one region to begin with. Particles move faster when warmer, so diffusion is faster in hot water; this fits the idea that the motion belongs to the particles themselves and is not an external push. In a real beaker, faster spreading in hot water can also be partly due to convection currents, so the demo supports the particle model but does not isolate diffusion on its own.

activities.title: Two-chamber particle simulation: net flow from random motion
steps: Load many particles onto one side of a two-chamber box divided by a membrane, leaving the other side empty, then start the motion.
Watch each particle jitter randomly while a concentration bar for each chamber ticks toward equal.
Slow the simulation and track individual particles crossing the membrane in BOTH directions.
State what produces the one-way NET flow even though individual motion is two-directional.
Continue until the bars are equal, and describe what the particles are doing at that point.
activities.insight: Individual particles cross the membrane randomly in both directions; the NET flow runs one way only because there are simply more particles on the crowded side. At equilibrium the two-way traffic balances, so net movement is zero while motion continues (dynamic equilibrium) — nothing is pushed and nothing stops.

activities.title: Deriving the three rate factors by controlled variation
steps: From a baseline simulation run, steepen the concentration gradient (add more particles to one side) and read whether the rate meter rises, holding the other settings fixed.
Separately, enlarge the membrane surface area only, and note the effect on rate.
Separately, thin the diffusion distance (thinner membrane) only, and note the effect on rate.
Record each result and state the three factors that speed diffusion up, each with a reason.
Order or compare two scenarios and predict which diffuses faster.
activities.insight: Diffusion rate increases with a steeper concentration gradient, a larger surface area, and a shorter diffusion distance; changing one factor at a time shows each as a genuine cause, not a memorised list.

activities.title: Apply the model to gas exchange and glucose supply
steps: Using a 'cell mode' overlay or an alveolus–capillary diagram, mark which way oxygen diffuses (air/alveolus → blood) and which way carbon dioxide diffuses (blood → air).
Justify each direction from the stated concentration difference (high → low).
Explain how a respiring cell obtains glucose from the blood by diffusion.
Name one feature of the gas-exchange surface that speeds diffusion (large surface area, thin membrane, maintained gradient) and say why.
activities.insight: The same particle model explains how the body moves materials: net movement is always from high to low concentration, so O₂ enters blood, CO₂ leaves, and glucose moves from blood into respiring cells, with real surfaces built to maximise rate.

activities.title: Predict-and-check quiz on direction and rate
steps: Answer: which way does O₂ diffuse at the alveolus, and which way does CO₂ go?
Use a slider to predict the relative rate of diffusion as the concentration gradient steepens.
Sort factors into 'speeds up' / 'slows down' categories (e.g. steeper gradient, larger surface area, shorter distance vs the opposites).
For each answer, give the reason, not just the choice.
activities.insight: Learners can reliably predict the direction of net movement and relate rate to the three factors, with reasons, after the simulation has built the underlying model.

checkQuestion: You drop a spot of coloured dye into a glass of still water and don't stir it. Over time the colour spreads until the whole glass is evenly coloured. Why does the dye spread out on its own — and why does it stop spreading once the colour is even?
checkAnswer: The dye particles move randomly in all directions; because they start crowded together (high concentration) there is a net movement outward to where there are fewer of them (low concentration) until they are evenly spread. It doesn't really stop — the random movement continues, but once evenly spread there is no NET movement in any direction (equilibrium). No stirring or energy input is needed.
